outcome: Since 26 January 2024 the planar unit-distance count has moved: an OpenAI internal model's construction (announced 20 May 2026) gives n-point planar sets with at least n^(1+δ) unit distances for infinitely many n, with δ > 0 absolute, which refutes the conjectured n^(1+O(1/log log n)) bound; Sawin (same day) made δ explicit at about 0.014, and later human and AI-assisted numerics pushed the explicit exponent to about 0.0357 (unverified). The O(n^(4/3)) upper bound, the exact maximum for each n, and the true order of growth remain open.
problem_asks: (1) For each n, the exact maximum number u(n) of unit-distance pairs (pairs of points at Euclidean distance exactly 1) that a set of n points in the Euclidean plane can determine. (2) The order of growth of u(n) as n tends to infinity, i.e. matching lower and upper bounds as a function of n. The plane is Euclidean, so norms other than the Euclidean one are outside the question. The frozen statement does not state the conjectured answer; the Erdős conjecture n^(1+o(1)) or n^(1+O(1/log log n)) is the literature's framing, not part of the bullet's wording. The erdosproblems.com #90 page, cited as the same question, asks a yes/no form: whether every n-point set has at most n^(1+O(1/log log n)) unit-distance pairs.

events.what_happened: Ágoston and Pálvölgyi, 'An improved constant factor for the unit distance problem', arXiv 2006.06285: the number of unit distances among n planar points is at most 1.94·n^(4/3), improving the previous bound of 8·n^(4/3). Exponent unchanged. Listed for completeness: it predates the window and moves only the constant.
events.revisions: v1 11 Jun 2020; v2 13 Oct 2020; v3 15 Dec 2021 (current). No journal listed on the arXiv page.
events.delivers: Upper bound u(n) ≤ 1.94·n^(4/3) for all n in the plane. Constant-factor only.
events.remains: The exponent 4/3 and the exact values of u(n); the lower bound.
events.direction: Upper-bound side: consistent with the conjectured small growth; does not change the exponent.

events.what_happened: Alon, Bucić and Sauermann, 'Unit and distinct distances in typical norms', arXiv 2302.09058: for almost all norms on R^d (Baire-categorical sense), at most (1/2)·d·n·log₂ n unit distances, essentially tight for every norm. This concerns typical norms, not the Euclidean plane; I record it as a neighbouring question.
events.revisions: v1 17 Feb 2023; v2 7 Nov 2024 (current).
events.delivers: For typical norms on R^d only: at most (1/2)·d·n·log₂ n unit distances. Says nothing about the Euclidean plane, whose unit-distance count is known to be n^(1+c/log log n) or more.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks for the Euclidean plane.
events.direction: Different question: a different class of norms. Does not cut for or against the Euclidean conjecture.

events.what_happened: Greilhuber, Schildkraut and Tidor, 'More unit distances in arbitrary norms', arXiv 2410.07557: for every norm on R^d (d ≥ 2) there are n-point sets with at least (d/2 − o(1))·n·log₂ n unit distances, matching the Alon–Bucić–Sauermann upper bound for typical norms. Applies to the Euclidean plane but only gives n log n there, weaker than the known n^(1+c/log log n).
events.revisions: v1 10 Oct 2024; v2 16 Jun 2025 (current). Journal reference Bull. Lond. Math. Soc. 57 (2025) 2885–2901.
events.delivers: Lower bound n log n for every norm on R^d, including the Euclidean norm on R^2, which is weaker than what is already known for the Euclidean case. Restricts nothing and extends nothing for the Euclidean plane.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks for the Euclidean plane.
events.direction: Different question for the Euclidean plane: arbitrary norms. Its Euclidean-plane content is weaker than Erdős's construction.

events.what_happened: Alexeev, Mixon and Parshall, 'The Erdős unit distance problem for small point sets', arXiv 2412.11914: improved upper bounds on the number of edges of unit-distance graphs on n vertices for each n in {16,…,30}; for n ≤ 21 the bounds match the best known lower bounds, and the densest unit-distance graphs are fully enumerated. Computational method: more efficient generation of F-free graphs and a custom algebraic embedder, not AI.
events.revisions: v1 16 Dec 2024; v2 12 Feb 2025 (minor changes). Ancillary graph6.txt under CC BY 4.0.
events.delivers: Determines u(n) exactly for n ≤ 21 (the upper bound on edges matches the best known lower bound and the extremal graphs are enumerated), and improves upper bounds for 16 ≤ n ≤ 30. Restricted to finitely many n; says nothing about the growth of u(n).
events.remains: u(n) for n ≥ 22 (exact values for 22–30 are not established by this abstract), and the order of growth of u(n).
events.directly_checkable: The ancillary graph6.txt lists the graphs; the unit-distance realisations are checked by the authors' custom embedder, which the abstract page does not describe in detail.
events.doubts: Computer-based result; correctness depends on the custom embedder and the F-free generation, which I did not check and found no independent check of.
events.direction: Moves exact small values of u(n), which are instances of the quantity asked for. Does not touch the asymptotic question.

events.what_happened: Currier and Solymosi, 'Many unit distances requires many directions', arXiv 2504.04208: a set of n points can determine only o(n^(4/3)) unit distances from at most O(n^(1/3)) directions. A restricted structural statement about direction count.
events.revisions: v1 5 Apr 2025 only (as read).
events.delivers: Restricted to point sets whose unit distances come from O(n^(1/3)) directions: at most o(n^(4/3)) such pairs. Does not bound the general count.
events.remains: The general bound u(n) = O(n^(4/3)) and the exact values; the direction-restricted case is only the subclass of few directions.
events.direction: Structural: consistent with the 4/3 benchmark. Does not move the exponent.

events.what_happened: Pach, Raz and Solymosi, 'Erdős's unit distance problem and rigidity', arXiv 2507.15679 (v1 21 Jul 2025): a structural result for point sets with nearly n^(4/3) unit distances, which reduces a possible improvement of the Spencer–Szemerédi–Trotter bound to a conjecture on rigid frameworks. The rigidity conjecture is conditional; a weaker version is reported established by Raz and Solymosi. Published in the SoCG 2026 proceedings (LIPIcs vol. 367, pp. 83:1–83:9, published 27 May 2026).
events.revisions: arXiv v1 only (21 Jul 2025). Conference version in SoCG 2026 proceedings, published 27 May 2026.
events.delivers: No unconditional change to the upper bound. Conditional: if the rigidity conjecture holds, the exponent improves below 4/3. The weaker rigidity statement (Raz–Solymosi) is partial progress toward the conjecture, not a bound on u(n).
events.remains: The upper bound exponent (4/3 still the best unconditional bound), the exact values of u(n), and the order of growth.

checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted to SoCG 2026 proceedings, published 27 May 2026. The DROPS page does not describe the refereeing.

events.direction: Conditional route toward improving the upper bound; cuts toward the conjectured small growth only if the conjecture holds.

events.what_happened: Lucas Aloisio, 'Rigidity-Induced Scaling Laws in Unit Distance Graphs: The Algebraic Collapse of Dense Substructures', arXiv 2601.18831 (single author, 5 pages). Claims a 'Flatness Lemma' (a configuration variety for a unit-distance K_{3,3} is singular and collapses, by symbolic elimination) and argues this effectively improves the O(n^(4/3)) upper bound 'for non-degenerate Euclidean configurations'. The extension to K_{4,4} is asserted. No exponent is stated.
events.revisions: v1 only, 25 Jan 2026 (as read).
events.delivers: Claims an upper-bound improvement restricted to non-degenerate Euclidean configurations, with no exponent. As stated, the restriction leaves the general maximum u(n) untouched.
events.remains: The general upper bound and the exact values; the restricted class in the claim.
events.directly_checkable: The Flatness Lemma is said to rest on symbolic computation, with a Python verification script as an ancillary file (per the comments field). I did not open that file.
events.doubts: Unreviewed preprint, and I found no public engagement with it. The claim rests on a symbolic-elimination lemma and an extension to K_{4,4} that the abstract asserts but does not prove. The abstract is the only part I read. Pach, Raz and Solymosi (2025) state that a general improvement reduces to a rigidity conjecture that is still open, and this claim does not address that conjecture.
events.direction: Claimed upper-bound improvement for a restricted class. Whether the restriction is a real limit on the bullet's quantity is for the judging pass.

events.what_happened: OpenAI announced on 20 May 2026 (blog 'model disproves discrete geometry conjecture', per secondary reports) and posted a PDF, 'Planar Point Sets with Many Unit Distances' (cdn.openai.com unit-distance-proof.pdf), with the argument. Result: there is an absolute δ > 0 and infinitely many n for which some n-point planar set has at least n^(1+δ) unit-distance pairs. The construction is number-theoretic: an infinite unramified tower of totally real number fields with 3-power Galois group, in which a fixed set of rational primes splits completely (existence by Golod–Shafarevich theory), with lattice-point and pigeonhole arguments. The OpenAI page (HTTP 403) and PDF (binary) were not readable to me; the content here is taken from the companion note, from Sawin's preprint and from Aaronson, Quanta and Gasarch as quoted.
events.revisions: Not established: I could not read the PDF's version history. The erdosproblems.com #90 page (last edited 20 May 2026) records the disproof and the problem statement was edited the same day, per the forum.
events.delivers: A lower bound: for infinitely many n there are n-point planar sets with at least n^(1+δ) unit distances, δ an absolute positive constant. As reported, the OpenAI argument does not state δ explicitly (Sawin: 'an inexplicit exponent greater than 1'). The companion note's digest makes it explicit at about 6.24×10⁻³⁸ for one parameter choice (its §2.1, eq. 2.2), and Aaronson reports ε ~ 10⁻³⁸. Restrictions: only a subsequence of n; the bound refutes the conjectured n^(1+O(1/log log n)) form for all n, since it exceeds it on infinitely many n.
events.remains: The exact maximum u(n) for each n; the true order of u(n) (the best known exponent lies between about 1.0358 (lower, from forum records, unverified) and 4/3 (upper, Spencer–Szemerédi–Trotter 1984)); the upper bound n^(4/3) is untouched.

checked_by.who: Noga Alon, Thomas F. Bloom, W. T. Gowers, Daniel Litt, Will Sawin, Arul Shankar, Jacob Tsimerman, Victor Wang, Melanie Matchett Wood (authors of the companion note, event 'alon-et-al-remarks-2026-05-20')
checked_by.qualification: Professional research mathematicians in combinatorics, number theory and geometry; Gowers is a Fields medallist and Litt was asked by OpenAI's Sellke and Sawhney to check correctness
checked_by.what_they_did: Wrote a 'short, digested, human-verified version' of the OpenAI argument and checked it step by step (companion note, abstract and §6)

Said 'I would have recommended acceptance without any hesitation' for the human-digested argument, and 'No previous AI-generated proof has come close to that' (quoted in Quanta; I did not see the original)
Reports the argument as 'several-page', and that 'on analysis by human experts, turned out to be correct'. Second-hand; he does not name the experts.

machine_checked.note: The plby/Erdos90 README says it 'contains a formal Lean proof of OpenAI's 2026 counterexample'; I did not confirm it is sorry-free. The lean-eval problem page https://lean-lang.org/eval/problems/erdos_unit_distance_conjecture_false/ shows a 'declaration uses sorry' warning alongside 'All goals completed', an internal inconsistency. A separate Aleph Prover formalisation (event 'aleph-prover-formalisation-2026-05-28') is conditional on two external textbook theorems.

events.directly_checkable: The family is not a single finite object, but each member is explicit once the number-field tower is fixed. The companion note's §2.1 gives the parameter formulae (r = 2·3·5·7·11·13·17, v = r/2, u = ⌈18r³/π⌉·r⁻²) and the exponent (eq. 2.2), which can be checked by hand or by computation.
events.doubts: (1) The OpenAI PDF was unreadable to me, so the claim rests on the companion note's account and on secondary reports. (2) The lean-eval problem page is internally inconsistent about sorry (see machine_checked). (3) The forum asks whether the changed wording on erdosproblems.com ('prove or disprove') alters the question; Bloom asked for clarification on 25 May 2026; I saw no answer. (4) One Italian news site says the proof is about 125 pages; unverified and not from a primary source. (5) The companion note's §11 (Wood) raises a citation concern: earlier related work is 'not appropriately referenced in Chat GPT's paper'.
events.direction: Cuts against the conjectured form of the answer: it exhibits sets with more unit distances than the n^(1+O(1/log log n)) bound Erdős conjectured, so the 'how many' question is answered in the negative for that conjectured form. It gives no exact value and does not move the 4/3 upper bound.
events.object: A family of planar n-point sets, one for each of infinitely many n, with at least n^(1+δ) unit-distance pairs for an absolute δ > 0. The sets are projections of lattice points in a number field from the Golod–Shafarevich tower, so the points are explicit once the tower is fixed. The existence of the infinite tower is non-constructive (Golod–Shafarevich), and the companion note's pigeonhole lemma (its Lemma 2.2, following an idea of Michel, Soundararajan, Ellenberg and Venkatesh) selects the points. The construction does not give a bound for every n.

events.what_happened: 'Remarks on the disproof of the unit distance conjecture', arXiv 2605.20695, by Alon, Bloom, Gowers, Litt, Sawin, Shankar, Tsimerman, Wang and Wood (19 pages by the PDF's page count). It presents 'a short, digested, human-verified version of the recent OpenAI-generated counterexample' with Theorem 1.1 (there is ε > 0 and point sets P_i with |P_i| → ∞ and at least |P_i|^(1+ε) unit distances), an explicit exponent for one parameter choice (§2.1, eq. 2.2: about 1 + 6.24×10⁻³⁸), and reflections on the result. It says the argument 'is a somewhat simplified, somewhat generalized version' of the AI proof, and credits ideas to Ellenberg–Venkatesh, Golod–Shafarevich and Hajir–Maire–Ramakrishna.

events.remains: Everything in problem_asks except the lower-bound exponent claim: the exact u(n), the upper bound 4/3, and the order for all n.

events.what_happened: Will Sawin, 'An explicit lower bound for the unit distance problem', arXiv 2605.20579 (sole author; v1 only, submitted 20 May 2026). Theorem 1: for arbitrarily large n there is an n-point planar set with at least n^(1.014114)/C unit-distance pairs, C an absolute constant. Method: algebraic number fields of large degree and small discriminant with many small-norm primes, via a Golod–Shafarevich argument. The paper says OpenAI's team 'proved the same result with an inexplicit exponent greater than 1' and that the paper 'makes the exponent explicit'.
events.revisions: v1 only (submitted 20 May 2026 00:37 UTC) as read.
events.delivers: Explicit exponent 1 + 0.014114 for the same family of constructions, for arbitrarily large n. An improvement on the exponent of the OpenAI construction, not on its existence claim. Restricted to a subsequence of n.
events.remains: The exact u(n); the upper bound 4/3; the order of u(n) for all n.
events.directly_checkable: Theorem 1's parameters (T, S_Q, k, R) and the Kronecker-symbol checks are described in §1 as computable in Sage; the parameter choice is said to be picked by 'trying a few values and taking the best one'. I did not run the code.
events.doubts: No independent referee report found. Public discussion on erdosproblems.com #90 (for example Bloom's 31 May 2026 post) engages with the number-field towers but gives no verification. Numerical parameter choices were not optimised further by the author (per forum: 'had not tried harder optimization').
events.direction: Same as the OpenAI event: cuts against the conjectured n^(1+O(1/log log n)) form, with an explicit positive exponent.
events.object: An n-point planar set with at least n^(1.014114)/C unit-distance pairs for arbitrarily large n, built from a number field of large degree with small discriminant and many small-norm primes (a Golod–Shafarevich tower). Explicit given the field, while the existence of the tower is non-constructive.

events.what_happened: Anthropic's engineer Sholto Douglas announced on X that Claude Mythos solves the unit-distance problem with a 'cute, simple proof'. A PDF writeup at www-cdn.anthropic.com was reported (title, from a search excerpt: 'Integral points on norm–one tori and the Erdős unit–distance exponent'). I fetched the PDF and it was unreadable, so the title and abstract come from a search excerpt only. The construction is reported (Tao's digest, Theorem 3) as n^(1+c/log log log n) for an absolute c > 0, weaker than OpenAI's n^(1+c). The Decoder reports the process: isolated Claude Code instances with Mythos access each received the problem, one instance summarised and distributed the partial solutions to further instances, and a proof version was 'prepared by Opus 4.7'.
events.revisions: Not established. The earliest dated report I found is The Decoder, 26 May 2026; the PDF's own date was not readable.
events.delivers: Claimed lower bound u(n) ≥ n^(1+c/log log log n) for an absolute c > 0, for infinitely many n (per Tao's digest). Weaker than OpenAI's n^(1+c): the excess exponent c/log log log n tends to zero. It still refutes the uniform-constant O(1/log log n) form.
events.remains: As the OpenAI event: exact u(n), the 4/3 upper bound, and the order of u(n).

events.what_happened: Michael T. M. Emmerich, 'Optimizing Explicit Unit-Distance Lower-Bound Certificates', arXiv 2606.03419 (sole author; v1 2 Jun 2026, v5 9 Jun 2026). Reports a tailored integer evolution strategy giving δ = 0.015263, 'supporting the cautious statement u(n) > n^1.0152', and the Emmerich–Cordella certificate giving u(n) > n^1.031 for #T = 67. The abstract says MathOverflow reports certificates above δ > 0.035 and beyond δ > 0.036, which may use modified constraint systems.
events.revisions: v1 2 Jun 2026; v2 3 Jun; v3 5 Jun; v4 8 Jun; v5 9 Jun 2026 (as read). Comments: 'Added a declaration on the use of AI'.
events.delivers: Explicit lower-bound certificates on the same construction: δ ≈ 0.015263 (u(n) > n^1.0152 for arbitrarily large n), and n^1.031 for a larger prime set. Restricted to this family; the abstract reports higher MathOverflow values that may not follow Sawin's constraint system.
events.remains: As Sawin's event.
events.directly_checkable: The certificate data and pipeline are described; Tseng's Zenodo package is cited as an independent certificate package.
events.doubts: The abstract says some MathOverflow improvements may rely on modified constraint systems that deviate from Sawin's formulation.
events.direction: Same as Sawin: cuts against the conjectured form, with explicit exponents.

events.delivers: Claimed explicit exponent 1.0360257. Withdrawn in effect: reported to contain mistakes.
events.remains: As Sawin's event.

events.what_happened: Logical Intelligence formalised the OpenAI disproof in Lean 4 with its agentic prover 'Aleph Prover' (blog dated 28 May 2026; the page metadata shows 24 Sep 2026). The formalisation is 33,087 lines using 252 Mathlib modules, and is 'conditional on 2 external textbook theorems', 'treated as trusted assumptions'. The Comparator tool is said to certify it matches the stated theorem with no hidden axioms. Named external reviewers: Sergey Galkin, Mark Obozov, Thomas L. Browning, Kevin Buzzard, Johan Commelin; internal: Michael Freedman, Michael Mulligan, Milo Moses. Buzzard found errors in the external theorem statements after one iteration, which were corrected.
events.revisions: Blog header 28 May 2026 vs page metadata 24 Sep 2026 (unresolved). Forum: an unconditional standalone file by JakeMallen (14 Sep 2026) reduces Lean code to about 540k lines, with two earlier axioms removed.
events.delivers: Formal verification of the OpenAI disproof (the formal statement is that of the OpenAI construction), conditional on two textbook theorems not yet in Mathlib. Establishes the argument is checkable in Lean given those inputs; it is not a new result.
events.remains: As the OpenAI event.

The lean-eval problem page 'erdos_unit_distance_conjecture_false' (lean-lang.org) states the Lean theorem: there exists δ > 0 such that for every N there exist n ≥ N and a finset P of n points in EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2) with n^(1+δ) ≤ unitDist P. The page shows a sorry warning and 'All goals completed'.
events.revisions: The repository page shows no commit date; the lean-eval page gives no date.

events.what_happened: Lean package 'ErdosUnitDistance' (author kim-em, repository kim-em/erdos-unit-distance; reservoir page last updated 27 Aug 2026) formalises Alpöge's disproof of the uniform-constant form of Erdős's conjecture: for every C > 0 and every N there exist n ≥ N and an n-point set P in R² with more than n^(1+C/log log n) unit-distance pairs. The package records that it was 'Formalized 2026-06-11 (one working day) by an orchestrated ensemble of Claude (Anthropic), Aristotle (Harmonic), and Codex (OpenAI)'. Dependencies named: Mathlib, PrimeNumberTheoremAnd, TauCeti.
events.revisions: Last updated 27 Aug 2026 (reservoir page).
events.delivers: A Lean-checked version of Alpöge's uniform-constant disproof. It refutes the O(1/log log n) form uniformly in the constant, but gives no power gain, so it does not refute the n^(1+o(1)) form.
events.remains: The power-gain question (the OpenAI construction's n^(1+δ)) is not addressed by this package; the exact u(n) and the upper bound.

machine_checked.note: Page states 'No sorry, no extra axioms'; audit lists [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]. A separate ErdosUnitDistanceComparator package is listed on reservoir.

events.doubts: The Alpöge one-page disproof itself was not found (see the Alpöge event), so this formalises a text I could not read.
events.direction: Refutes the uniform-constant O(1/log log n) form, consistent with the bullet's conjectured form; does not reach the n^(1+o(1)) question.
events.object: The family of n-point planar sets in the Alpöge construction, via multiquadratic fields Q(i, √q₀, …, √q_(g−1)) and prime-number-theorem-in-progressions input (per the package's module descriptions), with no power gain.
people: L. Alpöge (the one-page argument it formalises)

events.what_happened: L. Alpöge's 'one-page disproof of the uniform-constant form of Erdős's unit-distance conjecture', as described by the Lean package above. I did not find the one-page text or any arXiv listing, so the date, venue and content are known only through the formalisation's description.
events.delivers: Per the formalisation's description: for every C > 0 there are n with more than n^(1+C/log log n) unit distances, deliberately trading the power gain for elementary inputs (PNT in arithmetic progressions, multiquadratic fields). Refutes the uniform-constant form only.
events.remains: The power-gain question and the exact u(n).
events.doubts: Date unknown, so I cannot tell whether it predates the OpenAI announcement (a priority question). The one-pager was not read.

events.what_happened: erdosproblems.com #92 (the Erdős–Falconer k-equidistant variant) is marked 'DISPROVED: This has been solved in the negative', with the note that the unit-distance disproof also disproves this stronger form (per the search summary and the Lean page). Along the refuting sequence the unit-distance graph has average degree n^(Ω(1)), while Erdős–Falconer predicted at most n^(o(1)).
events.delivers: A stronger, different question (equidistant point sets, average degree), disproved along the same sequence. Not a resolution of the bullet's quantity itself.
events.remains: The bullet's quantity as stated.
events.doubts: I read this only from a search summary and the Lean page; I did not open erdosproblems.com/92.

events.what_happened: Panteleimon Rodis, 'Algorithmic exploration of the unit distance problem in the rational plane', arXiv 2606.29415 (v1 28 Jun 2026, v2 3 Sep 2026). Reports experimental evidence: an algorithm generating unit-distance graphs in the rational plane with a scaling exponent of 1.17, which the abstract says 'surpasses recent theoretical predictions'. The abstract gives no proved bound.
events.revisions: v1 28 Jun 2026; v2 3 Sep 2026 (current).
events.delivers: Experimental evidence only; no proved bound. If the 1.17 scaling were proved for points in the plane it would exceed the known exponent, so it is recorded as a claim, not a result.
events.remains: All of problem_asks.
events.directly_checkable: The algorithm is described; I did not run it.
events.doubts: Experimental, no proof. The abstract's 'surpasses recent theoretical predictions' is not supported by a stated theorem.
events.direction: Experimental evidence on the growth; no bound established.

events.what_happened: Shubhrajit Bhattacharya and Ritesh Goenka, 'Congruent copies of finite patterns in planar point sets', arXiv 2606.27352 (v1 25 Jun 2026). For a fixed finite planar pattern S, n-point sets with Ω_S(n^(1+δ_S)) congruent copies of S, δ_S > 0 depending on S, building on OpenAI's unit-distance result and using Sawin's quantitative number-field construction. The paper answers a question of Brass and Pach 'in a strong form'.
events.revisions: v1 only (as read).
events.delivers: Lower bound n^(1+δ_S) for the number of congruent copies of any fixed S. For S a pair of points at distance 1, this is the unit-distance count, so it contains the bullet's lower-bound form; I did not verify the specialisation. No numerical δ_S is given in the abstract.
events.remains: The exact u(n); the upper bound 4/3.
events.doubts: Single-author-pair preprint; no independent check found.
events.direction: Generalises the lower-bound construction to other shapes; for the two-point shape it coincides with the unit-distance count, cutting in the same direction as the OpenAI event.

events.what_happened: Terence Tao, 'A digestion of unit distance constructions', terrytao.wordpress.com (3 July 2026). Places three constructions on a common footing: Erdős's grid (d₁(P) ≫ n^(1+c/log log n), c near log 2); the OpenAI construction (Theorem 2: n^(1+c), with 0.03583… ≤ c ≤ 1/3 as the best known range, and 'the optimal value of c is still unknown'); and the Mythos construction (Theorem 3: n^(1+c/log log log n)). Says Golod–Shafarevich towers inserted into the Mythos construction 'can recover the full strength of Theorem 2'. States the 4/3 bound is best possible for parabolas, so any improvement for circles must exploit a property of the circle. Disclosure: 'AI tools were useful for providing initial summaries of these arguments, as well as on explaining various fundamentals of algebraic number theory to me.'
events.delivers: No new bound. An expository digest of the OpenAI and Mythos constructions, with Tao's statement of the best known range for c. Theorem 1 (Erdős) is described as 'not hard to turn the above heuristics into a rigorous argument'; the Mythos section is a sketch.
events.remains: As the OpenAI event.

events.doubts: Self-described as heuristic in parts; the Mythos section omits a technical issue ('which I will omit here').
events.direction: Explains the lower-bound constructions; does not change the status of the upper bound.
events.object: Expository description of the OpenAI and Mythos families (number-field towers, Minkowski's theorem for a short lattice vector, pigeonhole counting).

The abstract does not mention this case study.

disputes.summary: Whether the OpenAI argument is AI-generated or AI-assisted. The Computational Complexity post (Gasarch, 24 May 2026) says the Alon et al. note and OpenAI's announcement treat the proof as AI-generated, and reports Gary Marcus's position that it is AI-assisted (I did not read Marcus's post). The companion note says the argument was 'first mathematically generated in one shot' by the model and 'expositionally refined' with Codex, and that the single-split-prime idea is 'due to Will Sawin after he read GPT's proof'.

Who prompted the model. Aaronson says 'my former student Lijie Chen simply gave GPT the problem'. Sawin's preprint says 'a team at OpenAI, consisting of Lijie Chen using an internal OpenAI model', with Sellke and Sawhney verifying. Quanta says the author line of the OpenAI paper reads only 'OpenAI'. A forum commenter, reported by Gasarch, says the exact prompt appears in the paper; I did not see it.

Who gets credit for the explicit exponent: Sawin's paper (explicit ~1.014) reads GPT's proof, while Aaronson says 'Will Sawin, a human (!), improved GPT's construction'. The companion note credits the single-split-prime idea to Sawin 'after he read GPT's proof'.

Conflicting values for the best explicit exponent. Tao's optimisation page 84a gives 1.03583 (Naslund, 'Unverified', current best). The forum says Naslund's bound contained an error and the corrected value is about 1.0357. A spiderduckpig claim of 1.0360257 (3 June) was reported to contain mistakes. The Emmerich preprint abstract mentions MathOverflow values above 1.035 and 1.036 that may use modified constraints.

Whether the Mythos construction is independent of OpenAI's. The Decoder says Mythos 'frequently took a different route' than OpenAI's model; another outlet says it found the same path and a more concise proof; Litt calls it 'a bit worse'. Tao's digest says Mythos gives a weaker bound 'with less algebraic number theory'.

Wood (companion note §11) says some earlier related work is 'not appropriately referenced in Chat GPT's paper'. The OpenAI argument's priority over related number-theory work is therefore disputed in part.
Alpöge's one-page disproof of the uniform-constant form (undated, not found) may predate or postdate OpenAI's 20 May 2026 announcement; I could not place it. Its formalisation is dated 11 June 2026.

erdosproblems.com #90: the problem description and status were edited on 20 May 2026 (forum, BorisAlexeev). A forum user asked (25 May 2026) whether the changed wording 'prove or disprove' alters the original question; Bloom asked for clarification; no answer seen. The site's history log shows the disproof note in entries dated 2025-10-20 and 2026-05-13, which is inconsistent with a 20 May 2026 announcement; I did not resolve this.

summary: The problem asks for the exact maximum number of unit-distance pairs among n points in the Euclidean plane and its order of growth. Searches (43 in all) found a large, recent change in the lower-bound side. On 20 May 2026 OpenAI announced an internal model's construction giving n^(1+δ) unit distances for infinitely many n, with δ > 0. Its argument is number-theoretic (Golod–Shafarevich towers). The companion note by nine mathematicians (arXiv 2605.20695) gives a digested, human-verified version with an explicit exponent of about 6.24×10⁻³⁸ for one parameter choice, and says the first version was 'first mathematically generated in one shot by an internal model at OpenAI'. Sawin (arXiv 2605.20579, same day) gave an explicit exponent 1.014114. Later numerics, some attributed to ChatGPT 5.5 Pro by forum posters, reached about 1.0357 (corrected); a Tseng Zenodo package (23 May 2026) certifies 1.03158935 and says 'Generative AI made substantive contributions' without naming a model. Anthropic's Claude Mythos claim (reported 26 May 2026; PDF unreadable to me) gives n^(1+c/log log log n), which Tao digests on 3 July 2026 as a sketch. Lean formalisations exist: Aleph Prover (Logical Intelligence, conditional on two textbook theorems), plby/Erdos90 (sorry status unresolved), and kim-em's package for Alpöge's uniform-constant disproof (sorry-free, no extra axioms, dated 11 June 2026). The upper bound O(n^(4/3)) (Spencer–Szemerédi–Trotter 1984) is unchanged; the Pach–Raz–Solymosi rigidity route is conditional. Other 2025–2026 papers (Currier–Solymosi, Aloisio, Senger, Rodis, Bhattacharya–Goenka) are restricted, unreviewed, incomplete or about other questions. Exact small values (Alexeev–Mixon–Parshall, Dec 2024) are computer-based, not AI. Close calls: (1) whether the OpenAI result 'settles' the problem: it refutes the conjectured O(1/log log n) form but not the exact maximum or the 4/3 upper bound, so the outcome depends on how the judging pass reads a lower-bound exponent move; (2) whether the Mythos construction is substantively AI-produced: the authors' own sentence was not read, so the basis is secondary; (3) the Tseng 'Generative AI' statement names no system; (4) the status of Alpöge's one-pager is unknown and it may predate the OpenAI announcement; (5) whether the forum-reported ChatGPT numerics are load-bearing: they are unverified forum claims, and several have been corrected. AI involvement, on the authors' own accounts I read: the OpenAI argument (named as an internal model at OpenAI, and GPT in Aaronson and in the note), Codex used for exposition in the companion (not load-bearing), ChatGPT used for a literature reference in the companion (not load-bearing), Gemini for linguistic and LaTeX editing of Aloisio (not load-bearing), Claude/Aristotle/Codex in the kim-em formalisation (formalisation only), and Gemini 3.1 Pro in the Colosseum rediscovery draft (named by the authors, value of the draft not checked).
competing_reading: The strongest case for a different reading: the problem's status changed on 20 May 2026. OpenAI's construction, the nine-author digest, and the Lean formalisations together show that the conjectured Erdős bound n^(1+O(1/log log n)) (the form stated on erdosproblems.com #90, and the one the bullet's growth question is usually understood against) is false, and the forum records the problem as 'DISPROVED'. On that reading the problem counts as resolved in the negative for its conjectured form, and the events after it (Sawin, the numerics, Mythos) are refinements of a settled question, with the AI attribution of the OpenAI argument the main open point. The case against: the frozen bullet asks for the exact function u(n) and its order of growth, which the OpenAI result does not determine. It gives only a positive exponent for infinitely many n, leaves the O(n^(4/3)) upper bound standing, and says nothing about exact values; so on the bullet's own wording the problem is partly moved, not closed.
what_would_settle_it: (a) The OpenAI PDF text (unit-distance-proof.pdf) and the blog post, to read the authors' own account of how the argument was produced, the exact model name, and whether any human supplied the problem or steps; (b) Anthropic's PDF text, for Mythos's own account and whether its claim is complete; (c) the Alpöge one-page disproof, for its date (priority relative to 20 May 2026); (d) the Tseng Zenodo full description, for whether any model is named; (e) the MathOverflow thread 511514 and the forum history, for which exponent values stand; (f) whether the Google DeepMind formal-conjectures entry for #90 states the open problem or the disproof, and whether plby/Erdos90 is sorry-free; (g) the judging pass's own reading of whether a lower-bound exponent move counts as moving the quantity the bullet asks about.
